title: World Cup 2026: The Biggest Tournament in Football History
summary: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted across the United States, Canada, and Mexico, will be the largest in the tournament's history — 48 teams, 16 venues, three countries. We look at what to expect from football's greatest event.
content:
The FIFA World Cup has always been the biggest sporting event on the planet. The 2026 edition, co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico, takes that scale to a new level entirely. With 48 teams competing for the first time — up from 32 — and matches played across 16 venues in three countries spanning an entire continent, the 2026 World Cup is simply the largest football tournament ever staged.

The expansion to 48 teams has been controversial. Critics argue that it dilutes the quality of competition, that too many weak nations will participate, and that the tournament will lose the intensity that made the 32-team format so compelling. Supporters point to the commercial opportunities, the chance to grow football in new markets, and the simple excitement of more nations experiencing their first World Cup.

The Host Nations

The United States, Canada, and Mexico have each hosted the World Cup before — the US in 1994, Mexico in 1970 and 1986 — but never together, and never at this scale. The American venues include some of the world's largest stadiums: the MetLife Stadium in New York, SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles, AT&T Stadium in Dallas. Capacities of 80,000-plus will create atmospheres unlike anything regular football produces.

For the United States Soccer Federation, hosting the World Cup is a critical moment in the sport's development. American soccer has grown enormously since 1994, but the domestic game still competes for attention with the NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL. A successful World Cup on home soil — particularly one with deep American runs — could accelerate that development dramatically.

The Favourites

France, Brazil, Argentina, England, and Spain enter as the leading contenders. France's squad depth is extraordinary — they can field a competitive eleven from their substitutes alone. Brazil have rebuilt after disappointments and return with a generation of technically gifted forwards. Argentina, as reigning champions, carry the momentum of Messi's World Cup victory in 2022 — though questions about the squad's depth beyond their ageing superstar remain.

The World Cup is football at its most elemental — a tournament where anything can happen, where a nation nobody expected can go on a run that captures the imagination of the entire planet. That unpredictability is what makes it the greatest sporting event in the world.

The Dark Horses

Portugal, with Cristiano Ronaldo's era ending and a new generation emerging. Germany, rebuilding after their 2018 and 2022 humiliations. The United States, playing at home with a young squad that has genuine quality. Morocco, whose 2022 semi-final run proved that African football had arrived at the highest level.

What Makes a World Cup Special

The World Cup produces moments that no other tournament can replicate — the magnitude of the stage, the weight of national pride, and the fact that it comes only once every four years ensure that every match carries consequences that make hearts race in ways that club football, for all its quality, rarely matches. In 2026, that feeling arrives bigger than it has ever been before.
